extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, agents, and USPTO examiners
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and evaluative criteria used by the Federal Circuit and the USPTO for assessing patentability, claim interpretation, trademark registrability, practitioner discipline, and USPTO performance metrics. Includes case-law rules (obviousness, enablement, anticipation), procedural constraints (one-mark-per-application), and measuring metrics (pendency, cycle time).

rubrics_metrics.name: Motivation-to-combine requirement for obviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: The test of whether it would have been obvious to select specific teachings and combine them must be met by identifying some suggestion, teaching, or motivation in the prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Board findings must particularly identify any suggestion, teaching, or motivation to combine cited references; failure to make such specific findings cannot be supplemented on appeal (In re Dembiczak).

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplicity of prior art rarely weighs against obviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Simplicity of the prior art is rarely a characteristic that weighs against obviousness of a more complicated device with added function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although statements limiting the function or capability of a prior art device require consideration, mere simplicity of prior art does not ordinarily support nonobviousness of a more complex invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obviousness-type double patenting between design and utility patents
rubrics_metrics.description: Obviousness-type double patenting may be found between design and utility patents only in very rare cases where the claims of the two patents cross-read such that the subject matter of each would have been obvious from the other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A rejection is appropriate only if the claims of one patent would have made the other obvious and vice versa; absence of disclosure of specific designs in the utility claims precludes finding the design patents were obvious variants (In re Dembiczak).

rubrics_metrics.name: One-mark-per-application rule for trademark registration
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the Lanham Act and applicable regulations, a trademark application may seek to register only a single mark.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attempts to register 'phantom' marks (placeholders covering many possible substitutions) fail because they seek registration of multiple marks and encompass too many combinations to permit meaningful constructive notice or an effective search (In re International Flavors).

rubrics_metrics.name: Geographic misdescriptiveness bar to registration
rubrics_metrics.description: Geographically misdescriptive marks may be refused registration even with a disclaimer of the geographic term.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: With the NAFTA amendments to the Lanham Act, marks that are primarily geographically deceptively misdescriptive are precluded from registration under all circumstances; disclaimer does not permit registration of the whole mark if geographic misdescriptiveness is established (In re Wada).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonableness of PTO claim interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: The reasonableness of the PTO's claim interpretation should be assessed in light of the use of identical terms in other patents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where other issued patents use a term in a particular way, that usage can inform proper construction (example: 'restore' need not mean a return to the original state or a full head of hair) and can lead to reversal of a too-broad PTO construction (In re Cortright).

rubrics_metrics.name: Enablement and factual support under 35 U.S.C. §112 (¶1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims must be enabled by the specification; factual support must show that the claimed mechanism or active ingredient achieves the claimed result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rejections under §112 may be affirmed where the specification lacks adequate disclosure that the claimed active ingredient has the claimed effect (In re Cortright — claim 15 affirmed for lack of showing affecting hormone level).

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipation requires each claimed element to be disclosed expressly or inherently
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim reciting distinct elements is not anticipated by a prior art reference that discloses fewer physical elements even if the fewer elements perform similar functions, unless the missing element is expressly or inherently disclosed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims should be construed according to their language and the specification; if the claim requires three separate fastening means, prior art with only two combined elements does not anticipate (In re Robertson).

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim construction must respect claim language and specification statements about interchangeability
rubrics_metrics.description: Specification statements that describe elements as capable of being the same or serving multiple functions can affect how claims are construed (e.g., closure and disposal elements could be the same so long as complementary and engaged).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appellate construction may interpret claims to require separate elements or allow combined elements depending on claim language and specification; majority in Robertson construed claim to require three separate means based on claim language despite preferred embodiment disclosing three elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Board findings on motivation and other factual predicates are required and not supplementable on appeal
rubrics_metrics.description: When the Board makes a rejection based on combinations of references, it must make particular findings of fact identifying the suggestion or motivation to combine; appellate courts will not supplement missing factual findings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure by the Board to identify the specific suggestion, teaching, or motivation to combine references will result in reversal and remand (emphasized in In re Dembiczak).

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty of candor and practitioner discipline standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners owe a duty of candor to the PTO; knowingly relying on disavowed or fraudulent affidavits can result in public reprimand or other discipline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intent in disciplinary cases does not require direct evidence and may be inferred from circumstantial evidence; substantial evidence is required to support sanctions (Lipman v. Dickinson).

rubrics_metrics.name: USPTO performance and workload metrics (pendency and cycle time definitions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pendency and cycle time are measured metrics: 'average pendency' is the time between filing and issuance or abandonment (for utility/plant/reissue), pendency from original filing date vs most recent filing date differ (pendency based on most recent filing date; cycle time based on original filing date).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tables provide benchmark statistics (applications filed, first actions, disposals, allowed, abandoned, patents issued) and breakouts by technology center; pendency and cycle time are split into PTO time vs applicant time and reported in months. Notes clarify exclusions (e.g., design patents excluded from some averages).

rubrics_metrics.name: USPTO application processing stage metrics
rubrics_metrics.description: Pending application counts are tracked by stage: in preexamination processing, under examination, undocketed, awaiting first action, rejected awaiting response, amended awaiting action, in interference, on appeal, postexamination processing (awaiting issue fee, awaiting printing, D-10s).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These stage counts are used to summarize backlog and workflow and to identify bottlenecks in examination processing (Table 5 summary of pending patent applications).
